task_row_model.query: Design a lock-free, bounded-capacity LRU cache in Java that provides expected O(1) get and put under high contention and is linearizable. Describe the data structures, algorithms for get/put/eviction, how to manage memory reclamation safely in the JVM, strategies to mitigate contention, and give a sketch proof of linearizability identifying linearization points and key invariants.

documents.content: A common practical approach to a concurrent LRU in Java uses a ConcurrentHashMap<K,Node> for O(1) key lookups and a concurrent deque to track access order. Each Node holds the key, value and a stable identity reference placed into the deque. On access, the node is moved to the head: remove-if-present and offerFirst are attempted. Eviction checks the size and polls the tail, removing the last node and deleting its map entry. This design reduces global locking but can yield stale entries when moves race; correctness relies on atomic map operations and idempotent deque removals. Sharding the cache into multiple independent segments lowers contention and keeps per-segment operations fast.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarized an engineering pattern: pair ConcurrentHashMap for lookup with a concurrent deque for recency. Described node identity, move-to-front via removal and offer, eviction via tail poll and map removal. Mentioned races and sharding as contention mitigation. Focused on practical Java primitives (ConcurrentHashMap, concurrent deque) without formal proof.

documents.content: Tuning JVM garbage collectors can affect latency and throughput of concurrent data structures. Choose a collector with low pause semantics (e.g., ZGC, Shenandoah) for large heaps and pause-sensitive workloads. Reduce object churn by reusing objects where safe or using primitive arrays. Use escape analysis to let the JIT stack-allocate short-lived objects and avoid unnecessary allocations. Monitor GC logs, pause times, and allocation rates; correlate pauses with spikes in throughput. Although GC choice does not change algorithmic lock-free guarantees, it impacts observed latency under heavy allocation from temporary node objects or short-lived helper structures used during CAS retries.
documents.reasoning_trace: Outlined JVM GC choices and tuning advice relevant to latency-sensitive concurrent structures. Emphasized object churn reduction, escape analysis, and monitoring. Framed GC as an operational concern that influences performance but not algorithmic semantics.

documents.content: Proving linearizability typically uses identification of linearization points and establishing invariants preserved by atomic steps. For each operation, pick a single atomic action (successful CAS, map.putIfAbsent, or return of a map.get) as its linearization point; show that the effect at that point matches the sequential specification. Use helper invariants: every node returned by map.get is either marked removed or present in the ordering structure, and size counters reflect map membership. Forward simulation or reduction to known linearizable primitives can formalize correctness. Reason about concurrent removals by showing conflicting CAS sequences always leave state consistent and that each completed operation maps to a unique sequential event.
documents.reasoning_trace: Compressed standard proof methodology: choose linearization points (successful CAS or map operations), state key invariants about nodes and size, and recommend forward simulation or reduction techniques to formalize correctness. Kept discussion generic to apply to cache structures.

documents.content: One viable lock-free design shards capacity across S independent segments; each segment implements a non-blocking LRU with: ConcurrentHashMap<K,Node> map, Node {K key; V value; AtomicReference<Node> prev,next; AtomicMarkableReference<Node> removedFlag}, an atomic head/tail sentinel pair, and an AtomicInteger size. get: map.get(key) returns node; if non-null and not marked removed, attempt a CAS loop to splice node to head (update next/head links) and return value. put: use map.compute() or putIfAbsent to install node; if inserting, link to head with CAS; if existing, update value and move to head. Eviction: if size.increment returns > capacity, CAS-pop tail until a non-removed node is found, mark it removed, and remove from map via map.remove(key, node). Memory reclamation relies on the JVM GC: once node is unlinked and no live references remain, it is reclaimed; ensure no reuse of node identities to avoid ABA. Contention mitigation: shard to reduce hot-spotting, use backoff on CAS loops, and keep pointer updates minimal. Complexity: map ops are amortized O(1); deque splice/evict loops are expected O(1) under typical contention. Sketch linearizability proof: choose linearization points—successful map.get/putIfAbsent/compute result or the successful CAS that marks a node removed for eviction. Invariants: (1) map contains exactly the reachable non-removed nodes; (2) the ordering structure contains each non-removed node at most once; (3) size equals map.size(). Show each operation performs an atomic action that establishes the same effect as in a sequential LRU respecting those invariants; concurrent CAS retries only postpone but do not violate invariants, so forward simulation yields linearizability.
documents.reasoning_trace: Constructed a comprehensive design combining sharding with a lock-free per-segment structure: ConcurrentHashMap for lookup, atomic linked-node pointers, removed flag, and size counter. Detailed get/put/evict algorithms with CAS loops, JVM GC-based reclamation guidance, contention mitigation, complexity statement, and a linearizability sketch by picking clear linearization points and invariants.

documents.content: Filesystem journaling and block allocation algorithms focus on durability and crash recovery rather than in-memory concurrency semantics. A journaled filesystem records metadata updates in an append-only journal, commits batches atomically, and applies them to on-disk structures, ensuring consistency after power failures. Block allocation strategies (first-fit, best-fit, buddy allocator) balance fragmentation and allocation speed; journaling uses circular buffers and commit markers to bound journal size. These concerns are orthogonal to in-process lock-free caching; they influence persistence models and crash semantics if a cache must be made durable across restarts, but they do not prescribe in-memory non-blocking pointer algorithms or linearizability proofs.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarized filesystem journaling and block allocation concepts emphasizing durability and on-disk atomicity. Noted relation to persistence but deliberately focused away from in-memory concurrency primitives and linearizability.
